section_summary: This section covers Japanese bond imports into the Philippines, Australian wheat credits to Japan, and U.S. efforts to discourage further credits that might support Japan’s war in China. It also contains reports on Japanese government bonds and budgets, a clipping predicting financial strain, and most of a detailed June 1940 bulletin on Japan’s wartime public finances. The bulletin’s statistical appendix continues beyond page 186.

subfiles.title: Telegram on importation of Japanese bonds into the Philippines
subfiles.about: Reports the Securities and Exchange Commission’s view that proposed sales of unregistered Japanese bonds would fall under the Securities Act of 1933.
subfiles.summary: The telegram quotes the Commission’s General Counsel on the Act’s application in the Philippines. Mere importation is distinguished from offering, selling, or delivering the bonds after sale.

subfiles.title: Note on Japanese foreign debt service and trade balances
subfiles.about: Estimates Japan’s dollar and other foreign bond obligations against its adverse trade balances.
subfiles.summary: Estimates annual foreign debt service above $51 million and compares it with unfavorable U.S. and world trade balances.

subfiles.title: Comparison of Argentine and Brazilian dollar bonds
subfiles.about: Compares Argentine debt reductions and interest payments with Brazil’s proposed bond service.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that Argentina reduced its dollar debt and interest burden despite unfavorable U.S. trade balances, while Brazil’s favorable balances should permit more generous payments.

subfiles.title: Australian aide-mémoire on wheat sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Explains an Australian sale of 200,000 tons of wheat to Japan on 18 months’ credit.
subfiles.summary: Australia says it neither encouraged flour-credit negotiations nor approved further wheat-credit sales.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Australian Counselor Officer
subfiles.about: Records Officer’s delivery of the Australian aide-mémoire and his concern about competition from American flour sales.
subfiles.summary: Officer described Australian wheat-credit policy and said American official assistance to flour shippers disadvantaged Australian sellers. Hornbeck undertook to report his remarks.

subfiles.title: Confidential transmission of papers on Australian credits
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential papers about Australian credits for wheat flour purchases.
subfiles.summary: A damaged copy of an instruction transmitting background documents on credits to Japan, North China, and Dairen.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to the Consul General at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Sends documents about Australian credits for purchases of wheat flour.
subfiles.summary: Lists enclosed correspondence and memoranda for the consul general’s confidential information.

subfiles.title: Draft transmission of papers to the Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits documents on Australian credits to Japan, North China, and Dairen.
subfiles.summary: A damaged draft covering instruction listing enclosed correspondence about wheat-flour credits.

subfiles.title: Confidential instruction to the Ambassador in Tokyo
subfiles.about: Sends the Ambassador copies of documents concerning Australian wheat-flour credits.
subfiles.summary: Lists enclosed letters and conversation records for the Ambassador’s confidential information.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Herschel V. Johnson in London on credits to Japan
subfiles.from: A. A. Berle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains U.S. opposition to credits that might support Japan’s activities in China and requests reporting on British policy.
subfiles.summary: The Department cites Japanese exchange controls and injury to U.S. interests in China as reasons to discourage credits to Japan or for its use in China. Johnson is asked to follow British policy and, when appropriate, convey the substance of U.S. and Australian aide-mémoires orally.

subfiles.title: Instruction to the Consul General in Sydney on Australian credits
subfiles.from: A. A. Berle Jr., for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Requests close attention to further Australian credits to Japan and Japanese-controlled areas of China.
subfiles.summary: The Department restates its policy of discouraging credits that could aid Japanese military activity in China. The consul general is instructed to monitor Australian public and private lending and, if appropriate, stress U.S. concerns confidentially to Australian authorities.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese government bonds
subfiles.about: Points to a report on Japan’s December 1939 bond issue and annual bond float.
subfiles.summary: Records ¥660 million issued in December and ¥5.298 billion floated during 1939.

subfiles.title: Government finance excerpt on bond issues and note circulation
subfiles.about: Reports 1939 Japanese bond absorption, public debt, and a sharp rise in Bank of Japan notes.
subfiles.summary: Bond absorption weakened in the second half of 1939 as national debt more than doubled from its 1937 level. Bank of Japan note circulation reached a record high in December.

subfiles.title: Japan Financial: 1940–1941
subfiles.about: Argues that war budgets, bond financing, inflation, and foreign-exchange shortages threaten Japan’s capacity to continue fighting in China.
subfiles.summary: Ahlers describes a large projected budget deficit, heavy domestic bond issuance, rising Bank of Japan note circulation, and a shrinking gold reserve. He links exchange controls to shortages of industrial materials and consumer goods. The article predicts mounting economic strain and a possible need for Japan to withdraw from China.

subfiles.title: Embassy London despatch on Australian credits to Japan
subfiles.from: Herschel V. Johnson, for the Ambassador
subfiles.about: Reports a conversation with a British Treasury official about Australian credit and raw-material sales to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The official had been unaware of the 18-month wheat credit. He said Britain was trying to limit Japanese accumulation of Australian wool and other key Empire materials, though Australian preferences made this difficult.

subfiles.title: Government budget appropriations for fiscal year 1940–1941
subfiles.from: Harry I. T. Cresswell, Military Attaché, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes Japanese Diet appropriations for fiscal year 1940–1941 and compares them with the previous year.
subfiles.summary: The report itemizes general accounts, two supplementary budgets, and China war appropriations totaling about ¥10.56 billion. It notes reports of more than ¥15 billion in authorized expenditure, but says unclear special accounts and long-term military plans prevent a full accounting.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese government finance
subfiles.about: Points to a report on Japanese government finance in April 1940.
subfiles.summary: Identifies the original report and its file reference.

subfiles.title: Government finance excerpt for April 1940
subfiles.about: Reports a new Japanese bond issue, concerns about absorption, and rising note circulation.
subfiles.summary: April’s ¥400 million issue was better absorbed than March’s, while officials considered salary deductions for savings.

subfiles.title: Wartime Public Finance of Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes Japan’s prewar and wartime revenue, expenditure, taxation, debt, bond issues, and war costs.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin traces Japan’s prewar deficits and the expansion of military spending, then analyzes wartime tax reform, the general and special accounts, local finances, and the scale of government spending relative to national income. It estimates the direct cost of the China war through March 1940 at about ¥13.5 billion and describes how taxes, bond issues, and Bank of Japan underwriting financed the war. Its conclusion points to weakening bond absorption and growing pressure on capital and foreign-exchange resources. Pages 184–186 begin a statistical appendix that continues beyond this section.
